pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You used three kinds of constraints in the exercise: `comparable`, the `Number` union, and `fmt.Stringer`. What does each one let the function body do with `T`?
expected_points: comparable permits == and != — the same property required of map keys
a type-set union like ~int | ~int64 | ~float64 permits the operations all listed types share, e.g. arithmetic for Sum
a method interface like fmt.Stringer permits calling those methods on values of T
the constraint must grant every operation the body performs; any grants none

questions.prompt: The tests call `Sum` on a `[]Celsius` where `type Celsius float64`. Why does that compile — and what would break if `Number` said `float64` instead of `~float64`?
expected_points: Celsius is a distinct defined type, not float64
~float64 admits any type whose underlying type is float64
without the tilde the union lists exact types only, so Sum[Celsius] would fail to compile

questions.prompt: `DescribeAll` is generic over `[T fmt.Stringer]`. Why not declare it as `func DescribeAll(s []fmt.Stringer) []string`? And more generally, when do you pick a type parameter over an interface parameter?
expected_points: a []point is not a []fmt.Stringer — slices don't convert element-wise, callers would have to copy
interfaces suit varying behavior at runtime (io.Reader style); generics suit identical code over varying types
with generics all elements share one concrete type fixed at compile time

questions.prompt: The test writes `double := Map[int, int]` with explicit type arguments, but plain calls like `Map(nums, strconv.Itoa)` need none. Why the difference, and when else is explicit instantiation required?
expected_points: inference works from call arguments; a call's slice and function types pin down T and U
assigning or passing the generic function without calling it gives nothing to infer from
a type parameter appearing only in the return type also can't be inferred

questions.prompt: A teammate makes a helper generic 'for flexibility', but the codebase only ever instantiates it with one type. Argue for the simpler form — what are the signs a generic isn't earning its keep?
expected_points: one instantiation means the type parameter is pure cost — write the concrete type
generalize when real duplication with different types appears, not preemptively
readability of the signature matters; also prefer stdlib slices/maps helpers over hand-rolled generics

questions.prompt: Compare `IndexOf[T comparable]` with a pre-generics version taking `[]any`: where does each catch the mistake of searching a `[]int` for a `"string"`?
expected_points: the generic version rejects it at compile time — instantiation type-checks the call
the []any version compiles and only misbehaves at runtime (failed assertions or never-equal comparisons)
generics keep the compiler in the loop; no runtime type assertions in the body
